transcript:
Header: 2026-05-05 15:00 UTC; Duration ~70m; Recording: yes
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (CTO, Atlas), Diego Morales (Platform Eng), Aisha Khan (Security)

[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — networking topology for Private VPC, PrivateLink options, and then Marcus will walk through runtime perf and KV cache implications.
[00:18] Priya: Sounds good. We're particularly concerned about data egress and having everything stay in our account, plus low latency to our services in us-west-2.
[00:28] Marcus: Great. I'll try to tie both sides — infra and runtime. We'll show how prefix/KV cache affects RTT and some tradeoffs with batching and quantization.

[02:05] Diego: Quick note — we prefer no internet egress from model hosts, NAT gateways are limited by cost and we want PrivateLink if possible. Also our security team wants mutual TLS to Redwood control plane.
[02:23] Aisha: Yes, we need audit logs and we have strict egress rules; SOC2 also in scope.

[04:10] Marcus: Ok first, PrivateLink overview. For Redwood Private in your VPC we typically create an interface VPC endpoint backed by an NLB in Redwood's account, or we support a consumer-side interface endpoint to Redwood's service endpoint. That avoids internet egress; traffic stays over AWS network. A small caveat — PrivateLink uses ENIs so you'll see additional elastic IPs? Actually not EIPs, sorry, interface ENIs with private IPs in your subnets.
[04:45] Priya: So we create interface endpoints in our subnets and route to Redwood's service? Who manages the NLB?
[04:52] Sofia: For PrivateLink we host an NLB in our service account and you create the interface endpoints — commonly Redwood provides the service name and the NLB. Alternatively, for Dedicated installs inside your VPC we can deploy model hosts directly into your account.

[06:00] Diego: If we can't use PrivateLink, we'd have to egress via NAT to reach Redwood control plane — we worry about egress costs and also about predictable latency.
[06:15] Marcus: Right. NAT introduces asymmetric path and extra hops. For high-throughput low-latency inference work, PrivateLink is preferable because we avoid SNAT and it reduces jitter. But PrivateLink has some limits: you need interface endpoints in each AZ you want low-latency in; cross-AZ ENI traffic can still be routed. Also, remember there are per-ENI IPs and security groups bound to the endpoint.

[08:30] Aisha: How is DNS handled? We have private hosted zones and split-horizon DNS. We need Redwood endpoints to resolve to the interface endpoint IPs, not public addresses.
[08:44] Marcus: Two patterns: 1) You create a private hosted zone that maps the Redwood service FQDN to the endpoint IPs, or 2) use Route 53 resolver rules (Outbound endpoints + rules) to forward certain domains. We often recommend creating the private hosted zone and associating it with the VPCs. That way the SDK resolves to the PrivateLink addresses. Must ensure the TLS cert CN matches the service domain — Redwood will provide certs for the public domain and we can use SNI.

[10:12] Priya: What about NAT for model hosts that need to pull OS updates, model artifacts — can we restrict to S3 VPC endpoints?
[10:28] Marcus: Yes, we recommend S3 Gateway endpoints for artifact pulls, and ECR interface endpoints for container pulls. That reduces NAT usage. For other outbound only telemetry you can route via a proxy in a controlled subnet.

[12:05] Diego: On subnets: we plan private subnets for model instances, an infra subnet for control-plane ENIs, and a management subnet for ops. Any specific route table expectations?
[12:20] Marcus: Model private subnets should have route table to NAT (if you need outbound) or no default route if fully private with only interface endpoints. Control-plane ENIs (PrivateLink) need to be in subnets with free IP capacity and security groups that allow inbound from your client CIDRs. Also make sure your NACLs allow the ephemeral ports we use for health checks.

[14:00] Sofia: Let's pivot to runtime. Marcus?
[14:05] Marcus: Sure. Key runtime factors affecting latency/throughput: model size/quantization, batching policy (max batch size, latency SLO), KV cache effectiveness, and network RTT to KV cache or prefix cache store.
[14:28] Priya: Could you explain KV cache? We heard Redwood has prefix caching to reduce repeated compute for interactive sessions.
[14:37] Marcus: Absolutely. KV cache (or prefix cache) stores transformer KV states for previously seen tokens so when you continue a conversation we can reuse cached KV instead of recomputing. In practice, cache hits reduce token latency significantly — from ~60-90ms per token down to ~15-25ms on the same hardware in some workloads. The main tradeoff: the cache must be colocated or reachable at low latency. If cache is over PrivateLink inside the same AZ, hits are fast. If cache is remote and requires NAT crossing, you get extra latency.

[16:50] Diego: So we should co-locate cache and model hosts in same subnets/AZs?
[16:58] Marcus: Preferably yes. Redwood's private deployment allows deploying the cache service into your VPC so model hosts use local IPs. That minimizes cross-AZ latencies. Also consider cache size and eviction policy for long-running multi-user workloads.

[19:30] Priya: How does batching interact with latency SLOs? We need some predictions — our product is interactive chat with a 200ms target for first token.
[19:45] Marcus: If you aim 200ms FTT, you likely need small batch sizes or dynamic batching with strict time windows (e.g., 10-15ms wait). Larger batches increase throughput at the cost of tail latency. We can tune Redwood runtime batching: eager vs opportunistic batching, and use per-route configs. For fuzzy traffic you might use an early cutoff to ensure FTT. Also quantization can speed token throughput and reduce GPU memory but may affect quality slightly — that's another knob.

[22:40] Aisha: On quantization, do you support int8/4-bit and does that impact determinism or tracing for audit?
[22:52] Marcus: We support several quantization profiles; int8 usually has minimal quality impact on many LLMs, 4-bit can be more variable. For audit/tracing we still emit deterministic logs for inputs/outputs at the route level; internal kernel nondeterminism may exist but we can pin seeds for eval runs. If your compliance requires exact bit-level determinism, that's more involved.

[25:12] Priya: Any special security concerns with PrivateLink? We need RBAC to ensure only certain subnets can access model endpoints.
[25:22] Sofia: The interface endpoint enforces security groups; you can lock down which security groups or CIDRs can reach the endpoint. On top of that, Redwood supports token-based auth and mTLS for private deployments. Audit logs are available in the control plane and we can stream to your logging account.

[28:00] Diego: What about throughput — we expect bursts of 200 req/s with avg tokens per request of 60. How do batching and cache affect GPU utilization?
[28:18] Marcus: With good cache hit rate and batching tuned for throughput, a single p4d-like instance can handle significantly more requests; but in Private deployments throughput is bounded by instance count and kernel selection. We recommend running a small stress test: simulate 200 req/s with your token length and measure p50/p95 latency. Marcus will take that on as an action.

[30:50] Marcus: Practical note on ENIs and scaling: PrivateLink endpoints scale with ENIs, but each interface endpoint has quotas; also your AZ distribution matters. For autoscale we recommend at least two endpoints per AZ or monitoring for ENI exhaustion.

[33:40] Priya: DNS again — if we use split-horizon, how do we ensure SDKs don't cache DNS too aggressively and stick to old IPs during NLB failover?
[33:56] Marcus: Use low DNS TTLs on the private hosted zone and configure the runtime to respect TTLs. Also Redwood's clients support SNI and will re-resolve on TCP connection errors. For faster failover, you can include health-checked NLB targets.

[36:10] Aisha: KMS & key handling — how do model logs or cached payloads get encrypted at rest?
[36:20] Marcus: We support customer-managed keys for storage encryption in Private deployments. Cache stores and any persisted artifacts can be encrypted with your KMS. For in-flight we use TLS, and for mutual auth you can configure certs. We'll provide the doc for KMS integration.

[39:05] Sofia: Quick break-out — Marcus, can you show an example latency chart with and without KV cache?
[39:15] Marcus: (screen share described) Here's a synthetic: without cache, per-token latency clusters around 80-120ms; with cold cache miss it's higher, warm hits drop to ~18-30ms. Notice batching increases average token throughput but p95 can spike if you over-batch.

[44:00] Diego: For model artifact syncing — you mentioned S3 endpoints. If we lock down access, what's the recommended IAM pattern?
[44:10] Marcus: Use IAM roles for the model hosts and restrict S3 prefix access to the model artifacts bucket. Combine with VPC endpoint policies to restrict which principals can use the interface.

[46:30] Priya: About telemetry — we need logs to flow to our Splunk. Can Redwood push logs to an S3 bucket or Kinesis in our account?
[46:42] Sofia: Yes, for Private deploys we can configure log sinks to your account (S3, Kinesis, or CloudWatch) via a cross-account role or resource policy. We'll document options.

[49:20] Marcus: Some gotchas — NAT gateways have port exhaustion under high concurrent outbound. If model hosts need many outbound connections for dependencies, prefer VPC endpoints or an egress proxy pool. Also be mindful of NLB cross-zone costs if you put endpoints in single AZ.

[52:00] Diego: Bandwidth — any recommended instance types for high throughput?
[52:12] Marcus: Depends on model, but GPU families with high network bandwidth (e.g., A or P families on cloud) help. Also consider colocating KV cache within same instance group to avoid network hops. If you use separate cache cluster, ensure high NIC bandwidth (100Gb) for top-tier workloads.

[56:00] Aisha: Audit requirements — we need retention for logs and evidence that keys are rotated. Is that part of the Private offering?
[56:12] Sofia: Yes, enterprise packages include longer log retention and audit support; key rotation is possible through KMS policies. We'll include retention options in the docs.

[59:30] Priya: Ok wrapping up — what's the minimal pilot we can run to validate latency and security?
[59:45] Marcus: Minimal pilot: deploy 2 model hosts and a small KV cache within your VPC, create interface endpoints in two AZs, run a 10-minute stress test at your expected qps and token lengths. We'll instrument p50/p95 and GPU util. We'll also validate PrivateLink routing and TLS.

[63:00] Sofia: Recap of next steps: Sofia will send the Private VPC diagram and security docs; Marcus will schedule the benchmark run and provide a script; Diego will send VPC details. Any other asks?
[63:18] Priya: Please include example iptables/security group rules and the NLB target health-check config.
[63:26] Marcus: Yep will include sample security group rules and a recommended route table layout.

[65:00] Aisha: One last question — if we need full on-prem later, how much of this topology changes?
[65:10] Marcus: On-prem removes PrivateLink; you'd host everything inside your network and Redwood would provide an appliance or Helm charts that map similarly: private subnets, internal LB, and the same KV cache components. The networking primitives change but the principles (co-location, low-latency cache, secure TLS) remain.

[67:30] Sofia: Great call. We'll get docs out early next week and aim to schedule the benchmark for the week of May 11. Thanks all.

Action recap: Marcus to run benchmark; Diego to share network details; Sofia to send PrivateLink/NLB examples and SOC2/KMS docs.
